t.9.2: Things done and not done, and the pairs of opposites: when have they ever ceased, and for whom? Knowing this, here and now, through dispassion become one devoted to renunciation, free of vows.
t.9.4: All this is indeed impermanent, corrupted by the threefold suffering, without substance, contemptible, and fit to be abandoned; having ascertained this, one becomes tranquil.
t.9.3: Only for some rare blessed one, my dear, through observing the ways of the world, have the desire to live, the desire to enjoy, and the desire to know come to cessation.
t.9.6: Seeing the diverse opinions of the great seers, the saints, and likewise the yogins, what man, having attained dispassion, does not become tranquil?
t.9.5: What time is that, or what age, in which the pairs of opposites do not beset us humans? Disregarding them and living with whatever comes of itself, one would attain perfection.
t.9.8: See the modifications of the elements truly, as nothing but the elements; that very instant, freed from bondage, you will abide in your own true nature.
t.9.7: Is he not a guru who, having fully realized the true form of consciousness, carries one across the round of worldly existence by means of dispassion, equanimity and right reasoning?
t.9.9: Desires alone are saṃsāra; knowing this, let go of them all. The renunciation of that comes from the renunciation of desires; then abide, now, just as things are.
